lessons.title: Lesson 1: What smart home devices do
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name the common smart home devices and what each one can do for you.
This lesson builds toward: Given common smart home devices, you will name what a smart speaker, smart plug, smart bulb and video doorbell can each do, getting at least 3 of 4 right.
Smart home devices connect to your home Wi-Fi so you can control them by voice or with an app on your phone.
Common ones: a smart speaker, such as Amazon Echo with Alexa or Google Nest with Google Assistant, answers questions, plays music and radio, sets timers and reminders, and makes calls. A smart plug lets you turn a lamp or fan on and off by voice or on a schedule. Smart bulbs change brightness. A video doorbell lets you see who is at the door on your phone before you open it.
For older adults living alone, the most useful are often a speaker for reminders and calls, smart lights so you never walk into a dark room, and a video doorbell for safety.
Words to know:
- Smart device: a device that connects to the internet so you can control it by voice or phone.
- Wi-Fi: the wireless internet in your home.
- Smart plug: a plug adapter that lets you switch a lamp or appliance on and off by voice or app.
Try it now: Walk through your home and write down two daily jobs a smart device could make easier, such as turning on a hard-to-reach lamp or seeing who is at the door.
You can now name common smart home devices and how they could help you.

check.q: What does a smart plug do?
options: Lets you turn a lamp or fan on and off by voice or on a schedule
check.why: A smart plug controls whatever is plugged into it, by voice or schedule.

check.q: You live alone and worry about who is knocking at night. Which device helps most?
check.why: A video doorbell lets you see who is at the door on your phone before you open it.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Talking to a smart speaker
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Give clear spoken commands to a smart speaker or your phone's assistant.
This lesson builds toward: Using a smart speaker or your phone's voice assistant, you will give clear spoken commands that start with the wake word, so the device does what you asked, trying simpler words if needed.
You start a smart speaker with its wake word: "Alexa" for Amazon Echo, or "Hey Google" for Google Nest. A light shows that it is listening. Your phone's voice assistant works the same way with "Hey Siri" or "Hey Google".
Speak clearly, at a normal pace, and say exactly what you want: "Alexa, what is the weather today?" "Hey Google, set a timer for 15 minutes." "Alexa, play the classical music station." "Hey Google, call Margaret."
If it does not understand, say it again with simpler words. Newer speakers use AI to understand more natural questions, but short, clear commands still work best.
Step by step:
- Say the wake word: "Alexa" or "Hey Google".
- Wait for the light.
- Say exactly what you want, clearly.
- If it misunderstands, try again with simpler words.
Words to know:
- Wake word: the word that tells a smart speaker to start listening, like "Alexa".
- Command: a short spoken instruction, like "set a timer for 15 minutes".
Try it now: Using a smart speaker or your phone's assistant, give three commands: ask for today's weather, set a 5-minute timer, and ask for a reminder tomorrow at 9 am.
You can now give clear spoken commands to a smart speaker or voice assistant.

check.q: What is the wake word for Amazon Echo?
check.why: Amazon Echo listens for "Alexa"; Google Nest listens for "Hey Google".

check.q: You asked a long question and the speaker got it wrong. What do you do?
options: Say it again with shorter, simpler words
check.why: Short, clear commands still work best; try again with simpler words.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Setting up a simple routine
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Plan a routine that does several things with one phrase.
This lesson builds toward: Using the Alexa or Google Home app, you will plan and set up a daily routine that does several things with one phrase, with two or three actions, practiced by voice.
A routine lets one phrase do several things. For example, saying "Good morning" could turn on a lamp, tell you the weather and remind you to take your medicine.
Routines are set up in the device's phone app: the Alexa app for Echo, or the Google Home app for Nest. Look for a section called Routines, tap to add a new one, choose the phrase that starts it, then add the actions. Menus change from time to time, so if you cannot find it, check the app's help pages or ask a family member.
Start with one simple routine. You can ask an AI assistant to help you plan it: "Help me plan a morning routine for my smart speaker. I want the weather, a medicine reminder and my lamp turned on."
Step by step:
- Plan the phrase and the actions on paper.
- Open the Alexa app or Google Home app.
- Find Routines and add a new one.
- Choose the starting phrase.
- Add each action, save, and try it by voice.
Words to know:
- Routine: one phrase or time that makes a device do several things in a row.
- Companion app: the phone app that sets up and controls a smart device.
Try it now: Write down a "Good morning" or "Good night" routine with a phrase and two or three actions. Ask an AI assistant to check your plan and suggest one improvement.
You can now plan a simple smart home routine and know where to set it up.

check.q: What is a routine on a smart speaker?
options: One phrase that makes the device do several things
check.why: A routine lets one phrase, such as "Good morning", do several actions.

check.q: You cannot find Routines in the app because the menu changed. What do you do?
options: Check the app's help pages or ask a family member
check.why: Menus change from time to time; the help pages or a family member can show you where it is.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Smart devices for safety
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose smart home features that make living alone safer.
This lesson builds toward: Given the safety problems you want to solve at home, you will choose smart features that fit them and check what the product can and cannot do, before buying or relying on it. Given common smart home devices, you will name what a smart speaker, smart plug, smart bulb and video doorbell can each do, getting at least 3 of 4 right.
Smart devices can help you feel safer at home. Lights on a schedule or motion sensor mean you never walk into a dark room at night, which can help prevent falls. A video doorbell lets you see and talk to visitors without opening the door.
A smart speaker can call a family member by voice if you cannot reach your phone. Some speakers and services offer emergency features, but these vary by product and country, and not all can call 911. Check the product's own help pages to know exactly what yours can and cannot do. Medical alert devices made for emergencies are a separate choice to discuss with your family.
Before buying, make a list of the problems you want to solve, and ask a family member or a store helper which device fits. You do not need everything.
Step by step:
- List the safety problems you want to solve.
- Match each one to a device: lights, doorbell or speaker.
- Check the product's help pages for what it can and cannot do.
- Ask family or a store helper before buying.
Words to know:
- Motion sensor: a device that notices movement and can turn on a light.
- Medical alert device: a wearable button made to call for help in an emergency.
Try it now: Write down one safety worry you have at home, such as dark hallways at night, and the smart device that could help. Ask an AI assistant what questions to ask before buying it.
You can now choose smart home features that fit your safety needs.

check.q: How can lights on a motion sensor help you stay safe?
options: They turn on so you do not walk into a dark room
check.why: Lights that turn on by themselves can help prevent falls at night.

check.q: You want a speaker that can call for help in an emergency. What do you do before you rely on it?
options: Check the product's help pages for what it can and cannot do
check.why: Emergency features vary by product and country; check exactly what yours can do.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Protecting your privacy at home
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use the mute button and privacy settings on a smart device.
This lesson builds toward: When you want privacy at home, you will mute the microphone and review privacy settings and voice recordings, and share no texted codes or passwords with callers.
Smart speakers listen for their wake word. They may sometimes mistake another word for it and record a little. Cameras record video. So it is wise to know how to control them.
Every smart speaker has a microphone mute button; when muted, a light (often red) shows it is not listening. Use it during private conversations. Cameras often have a privacy mode or a cover. In the device's app, look for Privacy settings, where you can usually review and delete voice recordings.
Use a strong password for your Wi-Fi and for the device accounts, and never share the codes texted to you with anyone who calls about your devices.
Step by step:
- Find the microphone mute button on your speaker.
- Press it during private conversations; look for the colored light.
- Open the device app and find Privacy settings.
- Review and delete voice recordings if you wish.
- Use strong passwords and never share texted codes.
Words to know:
- Mute: to turn off a microphone so it cannot hear.
- Privacy settings: choices in an app about what is recorded, saved and shared.
Try it now: Find the mute button or setting on a smart speaker, or the microphone setting on your phone's assistant. Turn it off and on again, and notice how you can tell it is muted.
You can now mute a smart device and find its privacy settings.

check.q: Why might a smart speaker record a little by mistake?
options: It records everything all the time
It may mistake another word for its wake word
check.why: Speakers listen for the wake word and can sometimes mistake another word for it.

check.q: Your family is visiting and you want to talk about private money matters. What do you do with the speaker?
options: Press the microphone mute button and look for the light
check.why: The mute button stops the microphone; a light, often red, shows it is not listening.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Putting your smart home to work
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan and practice a complete daily routine.
This lesson builds toward: Using the Alexa or Google Home app, you will plan and set up a daily routine that does several things with one phrase, with two or three actions, practiced by voice. Using a smart speaker or your phone's voice assistant, you will give clear spoken commands that start with the wake word, so the device does what you asked, trying simpler words if needed.
Now put the pieces together. A good first routine is simple, useful every day, and easy to say.
Example: "Good morning" turns on the bedroom lamp, tells you the weather and your calendar, and reminds you to take your morning medicine. "Good night" turns off the lamps and sets your alarm.
Practice saying your routine a few times. If something does not work, check one action at a time in the app, or ask a family member to look with you. Keep a written note of your commands near the speaker until they become habit.
Step by step:
- Choose a phrase you will remember.
- Pick two or three useful actions.
- Set it up in the app, as far as your devices allow.
- Practice it by voice several times.
- Keep a note of your commands near the speaker.
Words to know:
- Habit: something you do so often it becomes automatic.
Try it now: Final task: write out your "Good morning" routine, set up as much of it as your devices allow, and practice it by voice. Then find and use the microphone mute button or setting.
You can now use voice commands and a simple routine to make your home easier and safer, while protecting your privacy.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Routine planned No written plan, or no starting phrase. A written routine with a starting phrase and two or three useful actions, such as weather, a medicine reminder and a lamp. The plan also includes a "Good night" routine. Routine set up Nothing set up on the device or phone. As much of the routine set up as the devices allow. Can say which actions the devices could not do and what to use instead. Clear voice commands The device did not respond to the commands. Practiced the routine by voice, starting with the wake word, and it worked. Wrote the commands on a note near the speaker. Microphone muted Could not find the mute button or setting. Found and used the mute button or setting and saw the light change. Also found where to review voice recordings in the app. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What makes a good first routine?
options: Simple, useful every day and easy to say
check.why: Start simple: a phrase you will remember with two or three useful actions.

check.q: Your new "Good night" routine turned off the lamps but did not set the alarm. What do you do?
options: Check that one action in the app, or look at it with a family member
check.why: If something does not work, check one action at a time in the app.
